Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Federated Cooperative Multi-Task Semantic Communication Thanks: This work was supported in part by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFTR) under Grant 16KISK016 (Open6GHub), and by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) – 518671822.

Ahmad Halimi Razlighi , Pallavi Dhingra2 , Edgar Beck , Bho Matthiesen , and Armin Dekorsy  Affiliation:  Affiliation: Department of Communications Engineering, University of Bremen, Germany Affiliation:  Affiliation: E-mails:{halimi, beck, matthiesen, dekorsy}@ant.uni-bremen.de Affiliation:  Affiliation: 2E-mail: pallavi1@uni-bremen.de Affiliation: 
Abstract

Task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom) prioritizes task execution over accurate symbol reconstruction and is well-suited to emerging intelligent applications. Cooperative multi-task SemCom (CMT-SemCom) further improves task execution performance. However, [1] demonstrates that cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive. Moreover, the existing CMT-SemCom framework is not directly applicable to distributed multi-user scenarios, such as non-terrestrial satellite networks, where each satellite employs an individual semantic encoder. In this paper, we extend our earlier CMT-SemCom framework to distributed settings by proposing a federated learning (FL) based CMT-SemCom that enables cooperative multi-tasking across distributed users. Moreover, to address performance degradation caused by negative information transfer among heterogeneous tasks, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method integrated in the FL process to ensure constructive cooperation based on an information-theoretic approach. Unlike common clustering methods that rely on high-dimensional data or feature space similarity, our proposed approach operates in the low-dimensional semantic domain to identify meaningful task relationships. Simulation results based on a LEO satellite network setup demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and performance gain over unclustered FL and individual single-task SemCom.

Index Terms: 
Multi-tasking, federated learning, multi-user, task clustering, non-terrestrial networks, LEO satellites.

I Introduction

Advances in artificial intelligence and end-to-end (E2E) learning-based system design have positioned semantic communication (SemCom) as a key enabler for next-generation wireless networks, especially 6G, which are expected to support a wide range of intelligent applications [2]. Unlike conventional communication paradigms that aim at accurate symbol reconstruction, these emerging applications prioritize task completion. SemCom addresses this shift by transmitting only task-relevant information [3].

Within the task-oriented SemCom literature, existing works can be broadly categorized into single-task [4, 5], and multi-task processing. Multi-task SemCom, improving model performance and generalization, further divides into non-cooperative and cooperative processing. Early studies consider non-cooperative settings where each task is learned independently using its respective datasets [6]. More recent works apply established multi-task learning (MTL) architectures [7] to the SemCom domain. For instance, [8] explores joint multi-tasking for SemCom systems exclusively based on machine learning (ML) approaches.

In contrast, previously we introduced an information-theoretic perspective on cooperative multi-tasking, moving beyond the black-box use of deep neural networks (DNNs) in [1]. We investigated a split structure for the semantic encoder, dividing it into a common unit (CU) and multiple specific units (SUs) to enable cooperative processing of multiple tasks. The resulting cooperative multi-task SemCom (CMT-SemCom) framework facilitated multi-tasking based on a single observation. Moreover, subsequent works extended this framework to scenarios with distributed partial observations [9] and to rate-limited wireless channels [10].

However, directly applying the existing CMT-SemCom framework to distributed multi-user scenarios, such as non-terrestrial networks (NTNs), e.g., low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks observing different regions of the Earth and operating with local datasets, is not feasible. This is due to the cooperation taking place at the transmitter side through the shared CU in the CMT-SemCom framework. LEO satellite networks are expected to play a central role in extending global connectivity and supporting intelligent services in future networks [11]. Moreover, in these networks, a single satellite or constellation may simultaneously support multiple tasks, like agricultural monitoring, weather prediction, and emergency response. Recent advances in onboard computation and hardware capabilities have made it feasible to deploy SemCom directly on satellites, allowing communication resources to be allocated towards task-oriented objectives [12]. Consequently, MTL and SemCom have recently become active research topics for satellite networks [13, 14, 15].

Motivated by these insights, we propose federated learning (FL) to enable cooperative, multi-task semantic communication in distributed, multi-user networks, e.g., satellite networks. FL has been widely studied in satellite systems [16] as it is considered an important step towards seamless integration of terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks for supporting various applications. Recently, FL has also been combined with SemCom for single-task scenarios [17]. Further, recent works have begun investigating MTL via FL using purely ML-based approaches [18, 19]. In this work, we extend our information-theoretic CMT-SemCom framework to distributed multi-user networks by incorporating FL as the mechanism for task cooperation.

In addition, existing multi-task SemCom, including the CMT-SemCom, commonly assume that all tasks are fully related, and applying these methods to unrelated tasks leads to suboptimal task execution and potential performance degradation. As demonstrated in [1], such a mismatched cooperation results in destructive cooperation, where unrelated tasks negatively impact each other’s performance. To address this issue, we introduce a semantic-aware task clustering mechanism in this work that groups tasks based on their semantic similarity. This clustering is integrated within the FL process, resulting in a clustered FL approach that improves task performance.

Thus, we propose a Clustered-Federated-CMT-SemCom framework, featuring a unified encoder on each semantic transmitter (Tx) and separate task-specific decoders on the receiver (Rx) side. Semantic Txs send only locally learned parameters to a parameter server (PS), which aggregates them using clustered FL to update the shared encoders. The proposed framework is trained E2E through alternating local training and communication rounds (CRs). The main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Proposing a Clustered-Federated-CMT-SemCom framework for distributed multi-user scenarios enabling cooperative multi-tasking.

  • •

    Introducing a semantic-aware task clustering mechanism to mitigate destructive cooperation.

  • •

    Leveraging an information-theoretic criterion in the semantic domain, moving beyond common clustering approaches that rely on data distribution.

II System Model

We consider a multi-user wireless SemCom system with FL-enabled cooperation. The overall system consists of two logical systems, the E2E SemCom and an FL mechanism that enables cooperative distributed learning.

The SemCom network consists of NN Tx-Rx pairs, each equipped with a single-antenna semantic encoder and a single-antenna semantic decoder. Each of these is associated with a downstream task. At the ii-th Tx, the semantic encoder observes a continuous-valued source 𝑺i\bm{S}_{i} and extracts task-specific information corresponding to the semantic variable Zi∈𝒵Z_{i}\in\mathcal{Z}, where all semantic variables share the same alphabet 𝒵={c1,c2,…,cf}\mathcal{Z}=\{c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{f}\}. The tuple (Zi,𝑺i)(Z_{i},\bm{S}_{i}) forms a semantic source, first introduced in [1] and fully described by the probability density function (pdf) p⁡(zi,𝒔i)p(z_{i},\bm{s}_{i}). Given an observation 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i}, the semantic encoder produces a channel input 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} of length dd according to the conditional pdf p⁡(𝒙i|𝒔i)p(\bm{x}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i}). The encoded signal is transmitted over an orthogonal additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The received signal at the ii-th decoder, after dd channel uses, is 𝒚i=𝒙i+𝒏i\bm{y}_{i}=\bm{x}_{i}+\bm{n}_{i} where 𝒏i∼N⁡(𝟎d,γn2​𝑰d)\bm{n}_{i}\sim N(\bm{0}_{d},\gamma_{n}^{2}\bm{I}_{d}). Based on 𝒚i\bm{y}_{i}, the semantic decoder infers an estimate z^i\hat{z}_{i} using p⁡(z^i|𝒚i)p(\hat{z}_{i}|\bm{y}_{i}) with the goal that z^i=zi\hat{z}_{i}=z_{i}. Thus, the ii-th SemCom link induces the joint pdf

p⁡(zi,𝒔i,𝒙i,𝒚i,z^i)=p⁡(𝒔i,zi)​p​(𝒙i|𝒔i)​p​(𝒚i|𝒙i)​p​(z^i|𝒚i).p(z_{i},\bm{s}_{i},\bm{x}_{i},\bm{y}_{i},\hat{z}_{i})=p(\bm{s}_{i},z_{i})\,p(\bm{x}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i})\,p(\bm{y}_{i}|\bm{x}_{i})\,p(\hat{z}_{i}|\bm{y}_{i}).

Following a data-driven approach, we consider that each SemCom Tx-Rx pair is trained from a local dataset 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i}, consisting of samples (zi,𝒔i)(z_{i},\bm{s}_{i}), available at the ii-th SemCom Tx. Note that during transmission, only 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i} is available at the encoder, while ziz_{i} is used for supervised training. We adopt a variational approximation technique in which the encoder and decoder pdfs are approximated by DNNs parameterized by 𝜽i\bm{\theta}_{i} and ϕi\bm{\phi}_{i}, respectively. While all encoders share the same DNN architecture, their model parameters may differ across tasks. The decoders are task-specific, and their DNN architecture depends on the corresponding task.

Our goal is to exploit cooperative multi-tasking benefits during training without collecting the datasets 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} at a centralized location. To this end, we leverage FL where the ii-th semantic encoder-decoder pair is trained locally from 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i}. This is an iterative process, where intermediate training results are synchronized using a PS at each CR. Since decoders do not share a common structure, only encoder model parameters participate in the FL process, and the decoders remain task-specific and local. Thus, a PS aggregates encoders’ parameters from a subset of semantically related tasks to prevent negative transfer across heterogeneous tasks. Let 𝒯={1,…,N}\mathcal{T}=\{1,\ldots,N\} denote the set of all tasks, and 𝒯k⊆𝒯\mathcal{T}_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{T} represent the kk-th task cluster. Then, the encoder model parameters of related tasks {𝜽i∣i∈𝒯k}\{\bm{\theta}_{i}\mid i\in\mathcal{T}_{k}\} are aggregated at the PS to form a shared semantic encoder model for cluster kk. Assuming KK task clusters, the PS maintains KK aggregated semantic encoder models. We further assume ideal communication channels between the semantic Txs and the PS during training. The aggregated encoder parameters are distributed back to the corresponding semantic encoders, enabling CMT-SemCom across related tasks.

III Semantic-Aware Clustered-Federated CMT-SemCom

We propose an efficient Clustered-Federated-CMT-SemCom for multi-user multi-task scenarios. This section introduces the Clustered-Federated-CMT-SemCom, which alternates between local training of semantic encoder-decoder pairs and periodic aggregation of KK unified encoders. Training is performed over multiple CRs, indexed by t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T. In each CR, local models are trained at the SemCom link for EE epochs, and the resulting parameters are transmitted to the PS for aggregation and global updating. Specifically, Section III-A formulates an InfoMax-based objective for local training, Section III-B describes the clustered FL-based aggregation and update procedure, and Section III-C presents our semantic-aware clustering mechanism that jointly determines the number of clusters KK and the associated task groupings 𝒯1,…,𝒯K\mathcal{T}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{T}_{K}.

III-A Local Training Objective

To design our local semantic encoder-decoder pairs, we formulate an optimization problem adopting the InfoMax principle together with the E2E learning manner as:

p⋆​(𝒙i|𝒔i)=arg​maxp⁡(𝐱i|𝐬i)⁡I​(𝐘i,Zi),p^{\star}(\bm{x}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i})=\argmax_{p(\bm{x}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i})}I(\bm{Y}_{i};Z_{i}), (1)

where the objective is to maximize the mutual information between the channel output 𝒀i\bm{Y}_{i} and the semantic variable ZiZ_{i}. Following similar steps as in [1], along with the fact that the encoder pdf is approximated by DNN parameters 𝜽i\bm{\theta}_{i}, the approximated objective function is derived as:

ℒi​(𝜽i)=I⁡(𝒀i,Zi)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{i}(\bm{\theta}_{i})=\,I(\bm{Y}_{i};Z_{i}) (2)
≈𝔼p⁡(𝒔i,zi)​[𝔼p𝜽i​(𝒙𝒊|𝒔𝒊)​{𝔼p⁡(𝒚i|𝒙i)​[log⁡p⁡(zi|𝒚i)]}].\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}_{p(\bm{s}_{i},z_{i})}\left[\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}_{i}}(\bm{x_{i}|\bm{s}_{i}})}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{p(\bm{y}_{i}|\bm{x}_{i})}\left[\,\log p(z_{i}|\bm{y}_{i})\right]\ \right\}\right].

Although p⁡(zi|𝒚i)p(z_{i}|\bm{y}_{i}) can be fully determined using the source and p𝜽i​(𝒙i|𝒔i)p_{\bm{\theta}_{i}}(\bm{x}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i}), due to high-demensional integrals we approximate it by pϕi​(zi|𝒚i)p_{\bm{\phi}_{i}}(z_{i}|\bm{y}_{i}). Thus, the objective is expressed as:

ℒi​(𝜽i,ϕi)=𝔼p⁡(𝒔i,zi)​[𝔼p𝜽i​(𝒚𝒊|𝒔𝒊)​[log⁡pϕi​(zi|𝒚i)]].\mathcal{L}_{i}(\bm{\theta}_{i},\bm{\phi}_{i})=\mathbb{E}_{p(\bm{s}_{i},z_{i})}\left[\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{\bm{\theta}_{i}}(\bm{y_{i}|\bm{s}_{i}})}\left[\,\log p_{\bm{\phi}_{i}}(z_{i}|\bm{y}_{i})\right]\ \right]. (3)

In (3), we emphasize the joint semantic and channel coding performed by the encoders as we consider p𝜽i​(𝒚i|𝒔i)=∫p𝜽i​(𝒙i|𝒔i)​p​(𝒚i|𝒙i)​d​𝒙ip_{\bm{\theta}_{i}}(\bm{y}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i})=\int p_{\bm{\theta}_{i}}(\bm{x}_{i}|\bm{s}_{i})\,p(\bm{y}_{i}|\bm{x}_{i})\,d\bm{x}_{i}. It also reflects our adaptation of E2E design, where we jointly optimize the encoders and decoders, including the wireless channel, as its transfer function is differentiable.

By replacing the source distribution p⁡(𝒔i,zi)p(\bm{s}_{i},z_{i}) with the corresponding training data set 𝒟i={(𝒔i(b),zi(b))}b=1|𝒟i|\mathcal{D}_{i}=\{(\bm{s}_{i}^{(b)},z_{i}^{(b)})\}_{b=1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{i}|} of size |𝒟i||\mathcal{D}_{i}|, and approximating the expectations using Monte Carlo sampling, we obtain the empirical estimate of the above objective function

ℒi​(𝜽𝒊,ϕ𝒊)≈1|𝒟i|​∑b=1|𝒟i|[1L​∑l=1L[log⁡pϕi​(zb|𝒚b,l)]],\mathcal{L}_{i}(\bm{\theta_{i}},\bm{\phi_{i}})\approx\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{i}|}\sum_{b=1}^{|\mathcal{D}_{i}|}\left[\,\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\bigg[\,\log p_{\bm{\phi}_{i}}(z_{b}|\bm{y}_{b,l})\bigg]\ \right], (4)

where we fix the sample size of the encoder output and the channel sampling 𝒚b,l=𝒙b+𝒏l\bm{y}_{b,l}=\bm{x}_{b}+\bm{n}_{l}, equal for each batch.

III-B Clustered FL Aggregation

With the local learning objectives in place, we now present the clustered FL aggregation and updating scheme for cooperative multi-tasking in multi-user environments. During each CR, two steps are performed iteratively. In the first step, the semantic encoder-decoder pairs are locally optimized based on the objective in (4). In the second step, at the tt-th CR, all locally trained encoders’ parameters {𝜽(t−1)}i\{\bm{\theta}^{(t-1)}\}_{i} are transmitted to the PS, and the aggregation takes place to update the KK unified semantic encoders as follows:

𝜽¯k=1|𝒯k|​∑i∈𝒯k𝜽i⋆k=1,…,K.\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{k}}\,\bm{\theta}^{\star}_{i}\qquad k=1,\ldots,K. (5)

In (5), 𝜽¯k\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{k} represents the aggregated semantic encoder parameters shared by all semantic encoders within the kk-th task cluster. Clusters {𝒯k}k=1K⋆\{\mathcal{T}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K^{\star}}, are constructed so that ⋃k=1K𝒯k=𝒯\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{T}_{k}=\mathcal{T}, ensuring that all participating encoders are included in the aggregation process, while 𝒯k∩𝒯k′=∅\mathcal{T}_{k}\cap\mathcal{T}_{k^{\prime}}=\emptyset for all k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime}, which enforces a disjoint cluster structure.

Consequently, the aggregation in (5) corresponds to a cluster-wise averaging of the locally trained encoder parameters, enabling constructive and cooperative multi-tasking. In Section III-C, we present the semantic-aware task clustering approach to determine optimal KK and 𝒯1,…,𝒯K\mathcal{T}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{T}_{K}.

III-C Semantic-Aware Task Clustering

Our goal is to characterize the relationships among heterogeneous tasks such that personalized global models are learned, as shown in (5), in order to guarantee constructive and cooperative multi-tasking among groups of semantic links. Therefore, for efficient MTL, we aim to group tasks based on their semantic relatedness, where semantic relatedness is defined by the similarity of the distributions of the underlying semantic variables 𝒁=[Z1,…,ZN]\bm{Z}=[\,Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{N}]\,.

A common information-theoretic measure of distributional similarity is the Kullback-Leiber (KL) divergence D(ℙ∥ℚ)D(\mathds{P}\|\mathds{Q}) with ℙ\mathds{P} and ℚ\mathds{Q} being arbitrary distributions. This suggests a clustering approach that groups tasks with mutually large KL-divergence together. However, a clustering metric should be symmetric and bounded. One symmetrization of the KL-divergence with these properties is the Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence [20], defined as

DJ​S(ℙ∥ℚ)=12D(ℙ∥𝕄)+12D(ℚ∥𝕄),D_{JS}(\mathds{P}\|\mathds{Q})=\frac{1}{2}D(\mathds{P}\|\mathds{M})+\frac{1}{2}D(\mathds{Q}\|\mathds{M}), (6)

where 𝕄\mathds{M} is the mixture distribution ℙ+ℚ2\frac{\mathds{P}+\mathds{Q}}{2}. The JS-divergence is nonnegative, takes the value zero if and only if ℙ=ℚ\mathds{P}=\mathds{Q}, and is upper-bounded by log⁡2\log 2. Since the JS-divergence quantifies how similar two distributions are to their average, it implies that these distributions become more similar to each other.

Computing the JS-divergence requires knowledge of the true distribution of 𝒁\bm{Z}. Since this information is unavailable, we obtain the empirical probability mass function (pmf) from 𝒟\mathcal{D} instead. Let the semantic variables alphabet, 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, then, for |𝒟i||\mathcal{D}_{i}| large enough,

pZi​(c)≈πi​(c)=∑𝒛∈𝒟i𝟏​(zi=c)|𝒟i|,p_{Z_{i}}(c)\approx\pi_{i}(c)=\frac{\sum_{\bm{z}\in\mathcal{D}_{i}}\bm{1}(z_{i}=c)}{|\mathcal{D}_{i}|}, (7)

for all ii and c∈𝒵c\in\mathcal{Z}. These empirical pmfs are computed on-device and are low-dimensional in comparison to the data dimension. The semantic Txs transmit their empirical πZi\pi_{Z_{i}} to the PS prior to the FL training process.

Next, we define the empirical semantic similarity ωi​j\omega_{ij} between ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j}, computed on the PS, as

ωi​j=1−12​∑c∈𝒵(πi​(c)​log⁡πi​(c)Ai​j​(c)+πj​(c)​log⁡πj​(c)Ai​j​(c)),\omega_{ij}=1-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{Z}}\left(\pi_{i}(c)\log\frac{\pi_{i}(c)}{A_{ij}(c)}+\pi_{j}(c)\log\frac{\pi_{j}(c)}{A_{ij}(c)}\right), (8)

with Ai​j​(c)=12​(πi​(c)+πj​(c))A_{ij}(c)=\frac{1}{2}(\pi_{i}(c)+\pi_{j}(c)). Due to the law of large numbers, ωi​j→1−DJ​S(Zi∥Zj)\omega_{ij}\to 1-D_{JS}(Z_{i}\|Z_{j}) as |𝒟|→∞|\mathcal{D}|\to\infty. Clearly, ωi​j=ωj​i\omega_{ij}=\omega_{ji} and 0≤ωi​j≤10\leq\omega_{ij}\leq 1 with ωi​j=1\omega_{ij}=1 if and only if ZiZ_{i} and ZjZ_{j} have the same distribution. Thus, tasks with semantic similarity ωi​j\omega_{ij} close to 1 should be grouped together, while tasks with ωi​j\omega_{ij} close 00 must not. We define 𝛀∈[0,1]N×N\bm{\Omega}\in[0,1]^{N\times N} as the semantic similarity matrix with entries ωi​j\omega_{ij}.

The clustering can be interpreted as a fully connected, undirected graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} with NN vertices representing Z1,Z2,…,ZNZ_{1},Z_{2},\ldots,Z_{N} and edge weights ωi​j\omega_{ij}. We want to cluster our related semantic variables such that each cluster keeps its full connectivity and no overlaps occur between the clusters. In other words, we want to remove all edges from 𝒢\mathcal{G} with small ωi​j\omega_{ij} and then identify the minimum number of fully connected subgraphs.

To induce this, we introduce a similarity threshold τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1), which acts as a design hyperparameter. Based on this τ\tau, we define a binary task–task relation matrix 𝐑∈{0,1}N×N\mathbf{R}\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N} based on 𝛀\bm{\Omega}, as its elements ri​j=1r_{ij}=1 if ωi​j≥τ\omega_{ij}\geq\tau, and 00 otherwise. To avoid overlaps, if task ii is grouped with task jj, and task jj is grouped with task kk, then task ii must also be grouped with task kk. Otherwise, tasks ii and kk could belong to different clusters that both include task jj, leading to overlap. To enforce this, we impose the transitivity constraint: ri​j+rj​k≤ri​k+1r_{ij}+r_{jk}\leq r_{ik}+1. This results in a block matrix of 𝐑\mathbf{R}, where the optimal number of clusters, K⋆K^{\star}, is identified by extracting the connected components in this matrix.

Further, the optimum clusters {𝒯k}k=1K⋆\{\mathcal{T}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K^{\star}} are also determined, without the need to transmit the local datasets to the PS. As a result, the clustered FL aggregation shown in (5) is implemented based on the semantic similarities, without requiring a priori specification of KK. The overall scheme of the proposed framework is presented in Algorithm 1.

IV Simulation Results

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, we apply it to a LEO satellite network scenario, as a representative use case, Fig. 1. We utilize the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, which contains 60,000 images for the training set and 10,000 images for the test set. The dataset is pre-processed by assigning multiple labels to each data sample 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i}, as we focus on a multi-label domain MTL. Thus, the label domain defines our 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and each label corresponds to a semantic variable ZiZ_{i}. Accordingly, the local datasets 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} available at each satellite, referred to as “Sat” in this section, is constructed as 𝒟i={(𝒔i(b),zi(b))}b=1|Di|\mathcal{D}_{i}=\{(\bm{s}^{(b)}_{i},z^{(b)}_{i})\}_{b=1}^{|D_{i}|}.

We consider three learning tasks: two binary classification tasks, classification of digit “22” as “Task1”, and classification of digit “66” as “Task3” in our setup. And one categorical classification task, which is the digit identification of {1,2}\{1,2\} as “Task2”. Therefore, the semantic variables are {z1,z3}\{z_{1},z_{3}\} ∼\sim Bernoulli and z2z_{2} ∼\sim Multinomial distributions.

To emulate realistic deployment conditions, the training data are distributed heterogeneously across the Sats, while maintaining approximately equal local dataset sizes, i.e., |D1|≃|D2|≃|D3|\mathcal{|}D_{1}|\simeq\mathcal{|}D_{2}|\simeq\mathcal{|}D_{3}|. All Sats use identical two-layer fully connected semantic encoders with ReLU activations and an output dimension of 88. Decoders are task-specific and differ only in their output dimensions, while the PS maintains the encoders architectures for aggregation without a decoder.

The number of DNN encoders instantiated at the PS depends on the number of task clusters K⋆K^{\star}. The task similarity threshold τ\tau, is determined by considering the middle points between the lowest and highest similarity scores in 𝛀\bm{\Omega}. Then, based on the proposed semantic-aware clustering method described in Section III-C, we obtain K⋆=2K^{\star}=2, where Task1 and Task2 form a shared cluster, and Task3 constitutes a separate cluster. The training procedure consists of 3030 CRs, each comprising 1010 local training epochs using the loss function in (4), resulting in a total of 300300 local training epochs per Sat.

To assess the performance of our framework, named as Clustered FL-CMT-SemCom, we compare its task execution accuracy against two baseline schemes: Unclustered FL-CMT-SemCom and Individual training. In the Unclustered FL-CMT-SemCom, locally trained model parameters are aggregated in a task-agnostic manner, without accounting for task clustering. The Individual training corresponds to single-task learning, where each task is trained independently, and no MTL is performed.

Fig. 2a and 2b show the rapid improvement and peak accuracy achieved by the proposed framework. These results demonstrate that cooperative multi-tasking improves task execution performance compared to individual training when semantically related tasks are jointly processed. Fig. 2c highlights the destructive cooperation in the unclustered setting where task-agnostic parameter aggregation leads to performance degradation relative to individual setting. We also observe that the proposed method is performing the same as the individual one, as it has been clustered alone. Finally, Fig. 3 presents the average performance across all tasks, showing that the proposed Clustered FL-CMT-SemCom consistently improves overall task execution accuracy across the network.

In addition, the results demonstrate that the proposed approach requires less FL communication exchange between the Sats and the PS to achieve higher accuracy, highlighting the communication efficiency it brings to the system.

V Conclusion

We extended CMT-SemCom to distributed multi-user scenarios, such as in non-terrestrial satellite networks, by introducing Clustered-Federated-CMT-SemCom. FL enables cooperative multi-tasking across distributed users, while an information-theoretic, semantic-aware task clustering ensures constructive cooperation among heterogeneous tasks. Simulation results show accuracy gains of up to 7.18%7.18\% and 4.77%4.77\% over the Unclustered FL-CMT-SemCom and Individual training benchmarks, respectively, along with faster convergence. Future work includes incorporating realistic wireless channels, studying the impact of noisy model updates, and developing more systematic semantic-aware clustering methods.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
